The first thing my mother put in the museum was a potato masher.

She wrote the label on the back of a gas bill: *Bent on the occasion of your father trying to open the bathroom window.*

“Why was he opening it with a potato masher?”

“The latch was stuck.”

“Why didn’t he use a screwdriver?”

“He had a potato masher.”

The museum occupied the narrow shelf above the washing machine. There was room for perhaps eleven objects, less if one of them was a hat. My mother had been given six months to live and had responded, in part, by becoming very particular about which nouns she used. The shelf was a museum. Her morphine was Tuesday. The hospice nurse, whose name was actually Grace, she called Grace, because, she said, you couldn’t improve on everything.

I told my brother about the museum on the phone.

“Is she doing that thing where she wants us to ask about Dad?”

I looked at the masher. My father had left when I was twelve. For a while he sent birthday cards with the ages of much younger children printed on them, altering the numbers in pen. On my sixteenth birthday I got a card that said *You’re 6!* with a slender blue one squeezed in.

“I think she wants us to ask about the masher,” I said.

The second exhibit was a sandstone-colored button, which my mother attributed to “one of those coats I hated but wore for twenty years.” The third was a set of keys she had found in a pear tree in 1989. She’d put a notice in the post office. A man had called to ask how high up they’d been. When she told him, he said they couldn’t be his.

“Did you ask why?”

“It was his dime,” she said. “I figured he’d tell me if he wanted to.”

On Thursday I brought a shoebox down from the attic. It contained our school pictures, my grandmother’s wedding license, and a blue ribbon my mother had won for a sponge cake at the county fair. I laid the ribbon on the shelf while she supervised from a folding chair.

“Not that,” she said.

“Why not?”

“It already says what it is.”

I turned it over. On the back, in pencil, someone had written *slight dip in center*. I showed her.

“Oh,” she said. “In that case.”

My brother arrived in late October with a carry-on bag and a paper sack of apples. He stood in the laundry room reading the labels. Then he picked up the potato masher and slid his thumb along the crooked handle.

“I did this,” he said.

My mother opened one eye. “Did you?”

“Dad was holding it. I stood on it.”

“What on earth for?”

“He told me to.”

He lowered one foot onto the base of the laundry hamper to show us how he’d done it. There was something so familiar about the care he took demonstrating this stupid thing that I suddenly wanted to be twelve again, to have the old privilege of telling him nobody cared. Instead I asked him if the window had opened.

“Oh, sure,” he said. “We broke it.”

My mother laughed until Grace had to come see what was going on. Later I asked if she wanted me to change the label.

“Put his name on it,” she said. “Don’t take your father’s off.”

My brother stayed. He made applesauce, which neither of us knew she disliked until she was too tired to be polite. We ate it ourselves, cold, standing in front of the refrigerator. On the last night there was a load of towels in the dryer. Every so often a metal zipper struck the drum. I kept thinking I ought to get up and stop it. I didn’t want to let go of her hand, and I didn’t want to ask my brother to let go of the other one.

In January we emptied the house. My brother took the masher. I took the keys. We left the folding chair out by the curb. A woman walking a spaniel sat in it while she waited for the dog to finish smelling the hedge. When I went out to tell her she could have the chair, she said she didn’t need it, but would I mind if she sat a little longer?

I said no. Then I went back inside and got the other chair, the good one we’d been meaning to sell.

We sat there in our coats. The dog finished with the hedge and came to inspect my boots. I had the keys in my pocket. They were on the kind of ring you have to pry apart with a thumbnail, and there was a little brass key among them that looked as though it had opened a diary or a cashbox.

I told her about the pear tree.

“How high up?” she asked.

Of course I didn’t know. It was the one part of the story I’d never thought to ask about.

“High enough that a man ruled himself out,” I said.

The woman considered this. “I lost a set of keys once,” she said, “and my husband said, ‘Where did you have them last?’ and I said, ‘If I knew that, Dennis, I wouldn’t have brought it up.’”

The dog sat on my foot. I could feel his warmth through the boot, which was surprising, as it was a very good boot.

“Did you find them?” I asked.

“Dennis did. In his coat.”

Across the street someone was bringing in the bins. The woman loosened the leash a little, and the dog settled more of his weight against my ankle. I’d spent the morning deciding what to do with the last of my mother’s things. There was still a broom in the kitchen, and a saucepan of water I’d put on for tea before remembering I’d packed the cups. In a minute I would go back in and turn off the stove. For now I asked her whether Dennis had had the decency to look embarrassed.
